_README: MARKER-ONLY. Never fetched by the student's browser until a teacher/marker PDF is generated (formative: automatically when the student clicks Generate; assessed: only via the ?teacher=1-gated action, after Final Submit). Never render any of this on the student-facing page. See CLAUDE.md §5's assessment-security amendment.

markingScheme.criterion: Cites at least one specific choice or result from their own delivery run or blood-sample scan (e.g. a specific vessel decision and what happened, or a specific component identified on the blood sample) as evidence, rather than a purely generic textbook statement.
markingScheme.accept: Any genuine reference to their own logged task/choice/result from the Investigation Record counts; exact wording not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: A general claim about arteries/capillaries with no reference at all to their own delivery run or blood sample.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly explains that arteries need thick, muscular, elastic walls because they carry blood at high pressure straight from the heart's contraction, and the wall withstands and smooths that pressure without bursting.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent scientific wording; the exact phrase 'elastic' is not required if the pressure-withstanding function is clearly stated.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly explains that capillary walls can be just one cell thick because capillaries are the site of exchange with cells, so a very thin wall lets oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide and waste diffuse across the shortest possible distance.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent wording naming diffusion and a short distance; does not need every named substance, one or two examples is enough.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating capillaries are 'thin' or 'small' with no mention of exchange/diffusion or distance.

markingScheme.criterion: Draws at least THREE genuine, well-matched parallels between real infrastructure and distinct circulatory parts (e.g. highway = artery, side street = capillary, depot/hub = heart).
markingScheme.accept: Any three sensible, clearly distinct real-world components each matched to a distinct circulatory part; the exact three named in the example are not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: Fewer than three parallels, or parallels that are too vague to tell which circulatory part is meant.

markingScheme.criterion: Links a blockage of their chosen real-world route to a real consequence for that system (deliveries/traffic stop reaching a destination).
markingScheme.accept: Any believable real-world consequence of a blocked route in the system they chose.
markingScheme.insufficient: States a route 'gets blocked' with no consequence described.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly explains WHY that consequence matches a real blocked blood vessel — a clot stopping oxygen and nutrients from reaching cells beyond the blockage — rather than just stating both situations are 'bad'.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement of the biological consequence of a clot (cells beyond it are starved of oxygen/nutrients) tied back to their chosen real-world parallel.
markingScheme.insufficient: Names 'a clot' without explaining what it actually stops from reaching cells.

criteria.source: Auto-marked from the Knowledge Check (auto_marked_score) — the teacher does not mark this row.
= the Explain question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (own evidence cited, artery mechanism, capillary mechanism). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: None of the three analytic points achieved: no reference to their own delivery run or blood sample, no correct explanation of why arteries need thick walls, and no correct explanation of why capillaries can be thin.

Achieves only ONE of the three: cites a specific choice/result from their own delivery run or blood sample OR correctly explains why arteries need thick, muscular walls OR correctly explains why capillaries can be one cell thick — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. cites their own evidence and correctly explains the artery mechanism, but the capillary explanation is missing or wrong (or explains both mechanisms correctly but never actually cites their own delivery run/blood sample as evidence).

Cites specific evidence from their own delivery run or blood sample, correctly explains why arteries need thick muscular walls to withstand high pressure, and correctly explains why capillaries can be one cell thick to allow a short diffusion distance for exchange — all three analytic points present.

criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (three real-world parallels, blockage consequence, mechanism explanation). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: None of the three analytic points achieved: no genuine real-world parallels drawn, no consequence of a blockage described, and no explanation of why that consequence matches a blocked blood vessel.

Achieves only ONE of the three: names at least three genuine real-world parallels to circulatory parts OR describes a believable consequence of a blocked route OR explains why that consequence matches what happens when a real blood vessel is blocked — the other two are missing or incorrect.

Achieves TWO of the three: e.g. names three real-world parallels and describes the consequence of a blockage, but does not go on to explain why that consequence matches a blocked blood vessel (or explains the biological mechanism without first drawing three clear parallels).

Names at least three genuine real-world parallels to circulatory parts, describes a believable consequence of a blocked route, and explains why that consequence matches what actually happens when a real blood vessel is blocked (cells beyond it are starved of oxygen and nutrients) — all three analytic points present.

criteria.source: Assessed holistically across BOTH the Explain and Apply answers together — independent of, and never overlapping with, the content marks in use_of_evidence and reasoning above.

levels.descriptor: Unclear or missing sentences; no scientific terms.
Understandable but with unclear phrasing or missing key terms.
Clear, well-formed sentences using correct scientific vocabulary (artery, vein, capillary, heart, blood).

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's markingScheme: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain markingScheme's 3 points, and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply markingScheme's 3 points — the rubric levels restate the same points as bands; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy (7 marks = full). Use the student's own logged delivery-run/blood-sample data (task/choice/result/detail/tries columns in simulation_results.trials) to verify any claim they make about their own run — do not take their prose summary on trust if it does not match their own logged data. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording per each point's 'accept' field; do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Report total, percentage, one strength, one correction, one next step, under 80 words.
